paragraphs.heading: From instructions to working parts
paragraphs.text: Gene expression is how a cell turns the information in a gene into a working product, either a protein or an RNA molecule that does a job of its own. It is what lets cells use their genes to carry out a huge range of tasks. Some genes are switched on all the time at a fairly steady level, while others are turned up or down as the cell's needs and surroundings change.

paragraphs.heading: Several steps
paragraphs.text: The process has several steps, and one of them is transcription, where an RNA copy of the gene's sequence is made from the DNA. For a gene that codes for a protein, that RNA is then translated into a chain of amino acids, which folds up into a protein. For a non-coding gene, the RNA itself is the useful product.

paragraphs.heading: Making the RNA copy
paragraphs.text: Transcription is carried out by RNA polymerases, which work by adding one RNA building block at a time to a growing strand. Each new piece matches its partner on the DNA template, except that the base uracil, U, takes the place of thymine, T. Bacteria use a single kind of RNA polymerase. Eukaryotes, working inside the nucleus, use three kinds, each needing a DNA region called a promoter and helper proteins called transcription factors to get started. Copying stops when the polymerase reaches a sequence called the terminator.

paragraphs.heading: Finishing the message
paragraphs.text: In prokaryotes, transcribing a protein-coding gene gives messenger RNA, or mRNA, that is ready for translation. In eukaryotes, the first copy, called pre-mRNA for a protein-coding gene, must be modified before it is mature. One change adds a cap to one end, the 5′ end, which protects the RNA from being broken down. Another cuts the other end, the 3′ end, and adds a tail of about 200 adenine bases, the poly(A) tail, which also guards it.

paragraphs.heading: Cutting and splicing
paragraphs.text: Most eukaryotic pre-mRNAs are made of alternating stretches called exons and introns. During splicing, a complex of RNA and protein called the spliceosome cuts out an intron and joins the neighbouring exons together. Sometimes particular exons or introns are kept in some copies and removed in others. This alternative splicing lets one gene give rise to several different transcripts, which may become different proteins.

paragraphs.heading: Why the nucleus matters
paragraphs.text: In prokaryotes, transcription and translation happen at the same time. In eukaryotes, the membrane around the nucleus keeps the two steps apart, which leaves time for the RNA to be processed. This extensive processing may have been an evolutionary advantage that the nucleus made possible.
